theme: Reproach has broken my heart, the suffering servant
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 69:1-21. A suffering man drowns in trouble, hated without cause, and mocked in his thirst. Notice the lines the New Testament applies to Jesus. Read it with the cross ahead of you.
settingTheScene: Psalm 69 is a psalm of David. It is one of the most quoted psalms in the New Testament, second only to Psalm 22 and Psalm 110 as a source of passages applied to Jesus. David pictures himself sinking in deep waters, hated by enemies, and abandoned by his family. He is a righteous sufferer. Yet he is also honest about his own sin. Jesus, who had no sin of his own, suffered all these things in a deeper way.
observation: “Save me, O God! For the waters have come up to my neck” (v. 1).
“More in number than the hairs of my head are those who hate me without cause” (v. 4).
“O God, you know my folly; the wrongs I have done are not hidden from you” (v. 5).
“For it is for your sake that I have borne reproach, that dishonor has covered my face” (v. 7).
“For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me” (v. 9).
“But as for me, my prayer is to you, O LORD. At an acceptable time, O God, in the abundance of your steadfast love answer me in your saving faithfulness” (v. 13).
“Reproaches have broken my heart, so that I am in despair. I looked for pity, but there was none, and for comforters, but I found none” (v. 20).
“They gave me poison for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink” (v. 21).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with a cry of desperation: “Save me, O God! For the waters have come up to my neck.” David is sinking in deep mud with no foothold. He is weary with crying out, and his eyes grow dim with waiting for God.

His enemies are many and hate him for no reason. “I must restore what I did not steal.” He is being blamed and made to pay for what he did not do. Then, honestly, he admits: “O God, you know my folly; the wrongs I have done are not hidden from you.” He is not claiming to be sinless, but he is claiming to be innocent of the charges against him. He prays that those who hope in God will not be put to shame because of him.

The reason for his suffering is devotion to God: “For it is for your sake that I have borne reproach.” His own family treat him as a stranger. “For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.” The disciples remembered the second half of this verse at the cleansing of the temple (John 2:17), and Paul applied the second half to Christ in Romans 15:3. Jesus bore the reproaches directed at God.

He prays at an acceptable time, in God’s abundant steadfast love, and asks to be rescued from the mire. “Let not the flood sweep over me, or the deep swallow me up.” He asks God to answer and draw near. “You know my reproach, and my shame and my dishonor; my foes are all known to you.”

Then verse 20: “Reproaches have broken my heart, so that I am in despair. I looked for pity, but there was none, and for comforters, but I found none.” The disciples fled in Gethsemane. No one comforted him. And verse 21: “They gave me poison for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink.” At the cross, Jesus said, “I thirst,” and was given sour wine. Matthew 27:34 and 48, and John 19:28-30, point back to this psalm.

The rest of the psalm (vv. 22 to 36) includes a harsh call for judgment on the enemies, and it ends in praise and hope. The righteous sufferer will be vindicated. We read the first half today to see the suffering that Jesus took on himself.
connection: Psalm 22 and Isaiah 53 are other great psalms and prophecies of the righteous sufferer. John 2:17, 15:25, and 19:28-30 quote or echo this psalm. Romans 15:3 quotes verse 9 and applies it to Christ. Acts 1:20 applies verse 25 to Judas. Matthew 27:34 and 27:48 note the sour wine. Lamentations 3:54 and Jonah 2:3-5 also speak of waters over the head. Hebrews 4:15 says we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize.
application:
When you feel you are sinking, pray verse 1 and verse 13 as your own.

Consider what it cost Jesus to bear reproach for God’s sake. Thank him in specific words.

Ask whether your zeal for God’s house is real. Bring it to the Lord in prayer.
prayerPrompts: Cry to God about what feels like drowning.
Thank Jesus for taking the reproach of those who reproached God.
Ask him to teach you to bear reproach for his sake.
